blocks.text: The account deliberately inventories Goliath’s bronze armor, leg protection, and javelin, along with the iron head of his spear. That attention makes the later contrast sharper: David declines Saul’s armor, approaches with his usual sling, and finally takes Goliath’s sword after the victory. Weapon materials, weight, and captured equipment are therefore part of how the scene is presented, not incidental detail.

This chapter stands within a larger movement in 1 Samuel: Eli’s failing priestly house gives way to Samuel’s prophetic leadership, Saul’s kingship is rejected, and David’s rise follows. David’s encounter with Goliath is thus one episode in the book’s developing account of leadership in Israel.

The David and Goliath account is preserved in substantially shorter ancient Greek and longer Masoretic forms. How those forms are literarily related remains disputed, so this information should not be used to settle the meaning of particular details without further argument.
